S tress and overwork rarely act in isolation. We saw in last week’s essay how hypertensive heart disease and related cardiovascular conditions lead to sudden, unexpected natural deaths. Stress accelerates the development of those conditions. This week, we will examine how these factors subtly change key structures within our blood vessels over time until they cause the catastrophic events which result. Not every stressed or overworked person dies suddenly; individual factors like genetics, existing hypertension, diabetes, obesity, smoking, alcohol use, and access to proper healthcare matter greatly. Reducing the risk involves addressing both the physiological effects of stress and the underlying cardiovascular vulnerabilities. These can be obtained by regular blood-pressure and metabolic screening; blood-pressure control if you are hypertensive; prioritising sleep and rest. Other measures are stress-management techniques, including simple ones such as structured downtime, physical activity, or social support. Avoidance of continuous overtime without recovery periods where possible is vital. Lastly, seek care for persistent symptoms rather than “pushing through” or invoking your faith. In short, stress and overwork are widely recognised as important but modifiable contributors that raise blood pressure and can trigger fatal events in men who already carry high rates of undiagnosed hypertension and related risks. Addressing economic and occupational pressures at a societal level, alongside individual health behaviour, must be part of the broader response. Therefore, you must conduct regular check-ups even when feeling well. Eating healthier diets with less salt and processed food, and early detection of hypertension and related risks, are the most important preventive measures any individual can take. While data quality on exact national rates is limited, due mostly to unreliable record-keeping, the figures available rely on hospital and autopsy series, surveys, and expert observation. The consistent finding across sources is that preventable cardiovascular events driven by hypertension and lifestyle factors are the core issue for sudden deaths in this demographic. Alcohol is a recognised contributing risk factor for the sudden deaths discussed among men under 50 in Nigeria, primarily through its effects on blood pressure, heart rhythm, and overall cardiovascular health. It is not usually the single dominant cause; hypertensive heart disease remains the leading finding in local autopsy series, but it amplifies existing risks, especially when combined with stress, overwork, poor diet, and undiagnosed hypertension. Cardiologists discussing the rise in sudden “slump and die” cases routinely list excessive alcohol consumption among the lifestyle drivers of hypertension, alongside stress, smoking, obesity, and sedentary habits. Advice for prevention almost always includes limiting or avoiding excess alcohol. Local studies support the blood-pressure link. For example, research on heavy consumers of traditional palm-wine liquor (“ozu”) found elevated blood-pressure parameters, particularly in middle-aged men. This is what alcohol does; excessive or regular heavy drinking is directly linked to hypertension. It can cause both acute increases through sympathetic activation and chronic elevation. Reducing intake often lowers blood pressure in heavy drinkers. Nigerian clinicians note that a substantial proportion of patients with hypertension, heart failure, or serious heart disease in outpatient clinics report significant alcohol use together with smoking. Binge drinking can provoke irregular heart rhythms including atrial fibrillation – “holiday heart syndrome” – and, less commonly, ventricular arrhythmias that can lead to cardiac arrest. This risk is higher in people who already have structural heart disease or hypertension. Long-term heavy use can contribute to alcoholic cardiomyopathy, causing weakening and enlargement of the heart muscle, which increases the chance of heart failure and sudden cardiac death in the long term. It also interacts with other lifestyle factors like obesity, poorer sleep, and reduced exercise. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Prevalence varies by region, age, and setting, but harmful patterns like heavy episodic drinking exist among adult men, even as some younger cohorts appear to drink less overall in recent surveys. The volume consumed matters. Light or occasional drinking has weaker or inconsistent links to sudden cardiac death in some global studies, but heavy or binge patterns are clearly harmful for blood pressure and arrhythmia risk. In a population with already high rates of undiagnosed hypertension, even moderate intake can be more problematic. Alcohol rarely acts alone. Its contribution is greatest when layered on top of hypertension, diabetes, obesity, smoking, chronic stress, and limited medical care. Limiting alcohol, ideally avoiding excess or binge drinking, is one of the straightforward lifestyle measures recommended alongside blood-pressure screening and control, better sleep, stress management, and reduced salt and processed food consumption. For men already under high economic or work pressure, substituting alcohol with healthier coping strategies can reduce one layer of cardiovascular strain. In summary, alcohol contributes meaningfully by elevating blood pressure and raising the chance of acute rhythm disturbances or progressive heart damage, particularly in the high-risk environment of undiagnosed hypertension and lifestyle pressures common among Nigerian men under 50. Reducing intake is a practical step that supports the broader prevention advice from physicians. Smoking, including cigarettes and even vaping, is another contributing risk factor for sudden deaths among men under 50 in Nigeria. It accelerates cardiovascular damage and raises the likelihood of acute events in people who already have high rates of undiagnosed or poorly controlled hypertension. Smoking increases that risk by damaging blood vessels and promoting atherosclerosis. Nicotine and other toxins cause endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and plaque build-up in arteries. This contributes to coronary artery disease, reduced blood flow to the heart, and higher chances of heart attack or cardiac arrest. This combination raises blood pressure and heart rate, causing temporary spikes in blood pressure. So, chronic use supports the development or worsening of hypertension. It also promotes clotting and arrhythmias. Smoking makes blood more likely to clot and can trigger irregular heart rhythms that may lead to cardiac arrest. These mechanisms are the dominant findings in Nigerian autopsies, and hypertensive heart disease and other risks such as stress, alcohol, obesity, and diabetes are the most likely combination of circumstances to cause sudden death in young Nigerian men. Smoking is rarely the sole cause in the local pattern of sudden unexpected natural deaths, where hypertensive heart disease predominates over classic coronary atherosclerosis (unlike in many high-income countries). Its impact is greatest when layered onto existing hypertension, diabetes, or other lifestyle pressures common in the demographic. Even so, it is one of the most actionable modifiable risks. Quitting reduces cardiovascular risk over time, with benefits beginning relatively soon after cessation. So, avoiding or quitting smoking cigarettes, shisha, or vapes is a standard recommendation from doctors, alongside blood-pressure screening and control, limiting alcohol, managing stress, better diet, and regular activity. For men under high work or economic pressure, eliminating smoking removes one major accelerator of the cardiovascular pathway that leads to many of these sudden deaths. In short, smoking meaningfully heightens the risk of the hypertension-related and arrhythmic events that drive sudden deaths in this group. It is a preventable contributor that sits alongside the stress, overwork, and alcohol factors already discussed. Questions and answers Sunday Doctor, thank you for your essay about Ebola some months ago. I have followed your column for many years and remember how you were the first to warn Nigerians about that disease in 2014. This time around, the same thing happened. God bless you. Continue the good work, sir. +2347******* Thank you very much for your comments and contribution. On both occasions, though, the speculated mode of entry into Nigeria did not happen as on the two occasions, diplomats were responsible each time for importing the virus. Sunday Doctor, I don’t know what is happening to me, but I always feel nauseous and have thick phlegm in my mouth. I don’t know why I can’t keep my saliva down, and I know that I am not pregnant. What should I do because I brush my mouth almost to the point of vomiting? 0806******* That is something that can happen occasionally depending on the state of your stomach. If you ate something not particularly in harmony with your stomach before the onset of these symptoms, a reaction like this is possible. So, to stop excessive secretion of saliva, you could try a medication like Buscopan over several days to gauge its effect. Sunday Doctor, I appreciate your good work on this column. I am a 31-year-old single woman. I get tired easily. This has been going on for nearly a year. I have seen different doctors who recommended many different tests, but nothing has been found except malaria parasites on two occasions. I have done a Google search of my symptoms and also used ChatGPT, and although the information is so much, one thing I haven’t done, which was suggested, is iron studies. Do you think I should do that too? 0806******* Good day to you. It is a good thing to be concerned about your situation. While there is no indication from your inquiry regarding which precise investigations you conducted, it is important to also consider hormonal studies in addition. Iron studies are unlikely to reveal anything of importance because it is expected that your doctors would have requested a full blood count on each occasion. That alone would have examined the nature, physical characteristics and numerical disposition of your red blood cells. Stool analysis, including for occult blood, is also important in case there is some lesion within your gastrointestinal tract that is responsible for some persistent blood loss that may not be visible. Sunday Doctor. I am 53 years old. The last time I menstruated was five months ago, and I was happy about it because it has been behaving like that for the past 1 year. Then, in the past 8 days, my breasts became heavy and painful, and I started to experience spotting. Sometimes, the blood comes out when it is not expected, and I am now wearing a panty liner anytime I am leaving the house. Is this normal? What should I do? Thank you. 08038******* To be clear, these events can happen. With the combination of your complaints, there is a probability that proper vaginal bleeding resembling your normal period could happen soon. That would likely provide you with some relief. You can use a mild pain reliever such as Paracetamol to deal with the breast discomfort, but this is not likely to be a serious event. However, if this happens to you up to 3 times in a row, you should see a gynaecologist. Sunday Doctor. When is the best time to deworm my twin five-year-old daughters? Should it be after they have eaten or before feeding? Thank you. 0803******* Worm expellers are better absorbed and more effective when taken on an empty stomach. The general advice is to be taken before breakfast. But in mass deworming campaigns, they are often administered to schoolchildren without following these recommendations. Sunday Doctor, thanks for past help. My right eye doesn’t see as clearly as my left eye, even with glasses, when reading. Small water blocks it, but when I clean it, it clears a little. Besides, objects are smaller than in the left eye when one eye is closed. I have used several eye drops and yeast tablets, but no luck. I am a 70-year-old male. 09039******* Good day, sir. If your eyes see the same object at different sizes, that problem will not be resolved with the use of eye drops and yeast tablets. You should get a proper examination by an ophthalmologist, and a solution will be found. Sunday Doctor, I think it is harmful for women to be taking contraceptive pills. It can be harmful in future, I think. What is your view? 0806******* Every medication has got side effects, but that is particularly true of contraceptives especially when they are used for more than two years. Dr. Sylvester Ikhisemojie
